<reason>Both sides were sharp and answered pressure questions with proper A1/A2 structure, but PRO kept a single stable frame (the "Buy" label misleads; who eats the loss) and neutralized each CON attack without shifting ground: the replication fear was answered with a clean "one license, one successor account, every generation" rule; the privacy objection was answered by pointing out paper shelves, diaries and browser history already pass by default and estate law handles exclusions; and the "waivable isn't a guarantee" trap was answered with a coherent floor-vs-menu distinction. CON's strongest material — priced portability as a market alternative, the sublicensing constraint, "mandate you can satisfy by deleting the product" — was genuinely damaging, but CON migrated from replication to service burden to sublicensing to server fragility, with the closing's "binds only future sales" and "servers in 2060" angles arriving late and asserted. Decisively, PRO's Q2 forced CON to say deceived existing buyers get restitution, and PRO's closing convincingly showed that per-title litigation by a widow is not a real remedy. Competitive but PRO made the choice easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A3.2/A5.2–A5.4 sequence: asking what the family of someone who already spent thousands actually receives, then turning CON's "refund, a claim, damages" answer into "the windfall, wearing a suit" — exposing that CON's alternative leaves the core loss uncured while CON's own "cheaper for platforms" framing conceded whose interests it served.</best_rebuttal>
